title: Creating and Using Multiple Objects
summary: Remove the #1 beginner doubt: 'If I write one class, can I make multiple objects?' Discover how independent objects live peacefully without mixing up their data.
learningObjectives: Instantiate multiple independent objects from the same class blueprint
Understand that each object has its own separate copy of instance variables
Predict program outputs when manipulating several objects in sequence
expectedOutcomes: Total confidence that modifying object A will never accidentally alter object B
Ability to build small multi-entity programs without confusion

activities.title: Three Houses on the Same Street

analogy.headline: House #1 paints their door red. Does House #2's door turn red?
analogy.story:
Imagine a suburban street where 3 houses were built from the exact same architectural floor plan.

- The owner of House #1 paints their front door **Bright Red**.
- The owner of House #2 paints their door **Sky Blue**.
- The owner of House #3 paints their door **Forest Green**.

Does painting House #1's door suddenly change House #2's door? Of course not! Even though both houses share the exact same floor plan (the class), each house is an independent physical structure with its own walls and its own door.

In Java, `student1`, `student2`, and `student3` are those three houses. Each holds its own unique state in memory.
analogy.keyTakeaway: A class is written once. Every object you create from it gets its own completely independent set of variables.

activities.title: Independent State in Memory

keyTakeaways: One class can spawn an unlimited number of independent objects
Each object created with 'new' gets its own private copy of all instance variables
Modifying fields on s1 has zero impact on s2, even though they share the same class
Two objects can have identical values while remaining two distinct entities in memory

activities.title: Working with 3 Independent Students
activities.description: Each student object neatly manages its own name, age, and course. When you call s1.display(), it prints Rahul's details. When you call s2.display(), it prints Priya's details. Zero confusion, zero variable collision!

questions.prompt: If you write 'Student s1 = new Student();' and 'Student s2 = new Student();', how many copies of the 'name' field exist in RAM?
options: Only 1 copy shared by all students
2 separate copies, one for s1 and one for s2
Zero copies until a method is called
questions.explanation: Every object instance receives its own separate set of instance variables.

hints.hint: Remember the houses on the same street.

questions.prompt: How many objects can you create from a single Java class blueprint?
options: As many as needed, limited only by your computer's available memory
Only as many as the number of methods in the class
questions.explanation: A class is a reusable template. You can create 1, 100, or 10,000 objects from it.

hints.hint: How many cookies can you cut with 1 cutter?

questions.explanation: Modifying s1.name has zero effect on s2.name. s2 holds its own independent value: "Priya".

hints.hint: s1 and s2 are separate objects in memory.

questions.prompt: What happens when 's1' and 's2' are created using 'new'?
options: Java allocates two distinct memory locations, one for each object
Java merges them into a single variable
questions.explanation: Each call to 'new' creates a completely distinct object instance in memory.

questions.prompt: Can two objects of the same class have the EXACT SAME values for all their fields?
options: Yes! Two different students can both be named 'Rahul' and aged 20, but they remain two distinct object instances
Only if they share the same variable name
questions.explanation: Two objects can have identical state values while remaining separate individual objects in memory.

hints.hint: Think of identical twins — two separate people!

questions.prompt: What is the danger of writing 's1 = s2;' by mistake?
options: It makes both variable names point to the SAME single object, losing s1's original object reference
It deletes the computer's operating system
questions.explanation: Assigning references ('s1 = s2') makes both variables point to the same object rather than copying field values.

hints.hint: Reference assignment connects two remotes to one TV.

questions.prompt: Why is object independence essential for an eCommerce shopping cart?
options: So User A adding an item to their cart does not accidentally add it to User B's cart!
Because web servers can only run 1 cart at a time
questions.explanation: Each user must have their own independent Cart object with isolated state.
50 + 80 = 130. Each car retains its own speed independently.

questions.prompt: If a class has 3 fields (name, age, course), how many total variables are created when you instantiate 4 objects?
questions.explanation: Each of the 4 objects gets its own set of 3 fields: 4 * 3 = 12 variables in total.

questions.prompt: True or False: Calling s1.display() can accidentally print s2's name.
options: False, when you call s1.display(), the method specifically uses s1's instance variables
True, but only if s1 and s2 were created in the same loop
True on Mac, False on Windows
questions.explanation: Calling a method on s1 operates strictly on s1's own instance data.

interviewQA.question: Do objects created from the same class share their instance variables?
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: No. Each object created from a class possesses its own independent copy of instance variables. Modifying an instance variable on one object has zero impact on other objects created from that same class.
keyPoints: Each object instance holds its own independent state
Instance variables are allocated separately for each object
Enables safe concurrent modeling of multiple entities

interviewQA.question: What happens in memory when you instantiate 100 Student objects?
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: Java allocates 100 distinct object blocks in memory. Each block contains its own personal copies of 'name', 'age', 'course', etc. The code for the class methods is shared, but the data is completely separate.
keyPoints: Instance data is completely isolated for all 100 objects

interviewQA.question: What is the difference between an object and an object reference variable?
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: The object is the actual block of data in memory created by 'new'. The reference variable (like 's1') is simply the named handle or pointer that stores the address of that object so your code can talk to it.
keyPoints: Reference variable = handle / pointer to that memory address

interviewQA.question: What happens when you write 's1 = s2;' in Java?
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: It copies the reference address from s2 to s1. Now both s1 and s2 point to the exact same single object instance! If you subsequently change s1.name, s2.name will also reflect that change because there is only one object.
keyPoints: Copies the reference pointer, NOT the object data
Both variables now point to the identical object

interviewQA.question: Can you store multiple objects in an array in Java?
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: Yes! Just as you can create an int[] array, you can create an array of objects, such as 'Student[] classroom = new Student[30];', allowing you to loop through and manage dozens of objects cleanly.
keyPoints: Object arrays hold references to instances
Enables scalable iteration over collections of objects

interviewQA.question: How does object independence prevent bugs in enterprise software?
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: In a banking server with 10,000 active sessions, each user is represented by an independent UserSession object. Because each session holds isolated state, User A's transactions cannot leak into or corrupt User B's account balance.
keyPoints: Guarantees data isolation across concurrent users

activities.title: Lesson 6 Checkpoint
checklist: I understand that creating multiple objects from one class creates multiple independent states.
I know that changing a field on s1 will never affect s2.
I can create 3 or more distinct objects and display their information cleanly.

• Rectangle 2: width = `7.0`, height = `3.0` (Area = `21.0`)

Demonstrate that changing Rectangle 1 has zero effect on Rectangle 2.
